newsitem.title: UK: EU-IATA informal talks on price consultation ban.
newsitem.headline: EU-IATA informal talks on price consultation ban.

text.p: The European Commission's decision in July to ban price consultations between air cargo companies within the European Union was being discussed on Wednesday at informal talks in Brussels between EC and international airline officials, industry sources said.
The talks with representatives from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) form part of ongoing discussions since July, the sources added.

The Commission's decision, which takes effect on June 30 next year would bring to end a block exemption to EU competition rules granted in 1993. This was done on the understanding that it would give rise to cargo interlining agreements within the EU.
Interlining permits two airlines to agree on a single tariff and share receipts for the transport of goods involving more than one carrier.
It involves four to five percent of intra-European airfreight according to EU Commission figures, although IATA believes the figure is closer to 11 percent of traffic.
The sources said IATA has decided "in principle to apply for an individual exemption", a suggestion first mooted in July.
However this is likely to be more limited in scope than the block exemption, and the conditions attached by the Commission will influence whether it is acceptable to airlines or not, they added.
IATA is still keen to have a published IATA tariffs for interlining reference purposes so that airlines are able to provide prices to all destinations.
Export industry sources said they queried why any formal IATA tariffs were needed for airfreight.
"Airlines should publish their own actual market rates, providing greater transparency for the whole airfreight market," they said.
Meanwhile Britain's Freight Transport Association (FTA) reviewing the Commission's July decision in its September bulletin said.

"With published airline rates, one is able clearly to compare rates being offered to forwarders and shippers (exporters), alike. Rebates and commissions negotiated by either party would remain confidential and depend on such things as volume commitments and the negotiatings skills of those involved."
"Along with charges for services rendered, this should be where an efficient forwarder or airline makes and earns its profit," it added.
